Today, I wanted to focus on Black Tampa in the 1880s and 1890s, a period where we really begin to see Black people trying to define themselves and freedom. When we look at the newspapers from that time, we see conversations that still sound familiar today. Articles criticizing Black women because their daughters were no longer being trained strictly for domestic labor. Public debates over whether the terms negro or colored should be used as the Black identity. At the same time we see Black people creating joy, community and social life through picnics, clubs, and organizations. One picnic location being the springs as described here. If you are wondering Where That Place is, it is the body of water near armature works, now known as ulele springs renamed in 2006, the citizens of Tampa, White citizens, did not favor Mr. James Magbee, a White man, By The Way. Thats another story when we get to who and why Tampa named certain things after people. But these gatherings mattered. Black people were building community in the public during a time when freedom itself was still being negotiated. We also see Black people stepping into leadership positions here in Tampa. Armwood served as one of the citys first police Black officers alongside three others. Joseph A. Walker served on the City Council. Earlier, Black councilman like sigh res charles -- sorry, after like Cyrus Charles and Henry Bromick. Politically, many Black residents aligned with Republican Party, which newspapers today -- I mean, during that time openly called the Negro Party. Democrats at the time were described as the party of aristocrats while Republicans were seen as the party of laborers and working people.
